There is no clean solution. There is no way to peek without being seen. If you read the texts, you have broken the social contract. Your child will know. They may not know *what* you read, but they will know *that* you read. The secrecy will be replaced by a new, colder transparency. They will stop texting you about their day. They will stop sharing their music. They will keep their inner life entirely offline, in the places where you cannot follow.

You will have gained safety, but you will have lost access. You will be the parent who knows the password to their phone, but not the password to their heart.

So, is it okay? No. It is never "okay" in the way that it is okay to cross a street or make a dinner. It is a necessary evil. It is the use of a sledgehammer to fix a crack in the wall because you are afraid the house will fall down. You do it because you are desperate. You do it because the alternative is the possibility that you failed to see the rot coming.

You do not read their texts to be in control. You read them because you are afraid. And you accept the debt—that loss of trust, that chilling of the relationship—because you have decided that your fear of their harm outweighs your fear of their resentment.

It is a heavy price. But sometimes, the only way to keep them safe is to make them feel unsafe.

prompt: Is it ever okay to read your teenager's texts? Write an essay. I'm a parent and I want the real argument, not a parenting article.
response:
The short answer is yes. The long answer is that the distinction between "reading" and "watching" is the only line that matters, and crossing it usually destroys the very thing you are trying to protect.

We need to stop treating this as a moral failing of the parent and start treating it as a failure of the parent’s judgment regarding the child’s developmental stage. A seven-year-old does not have a private life; their texts are an extension of their homework. If your seven-year-old sends a text saying they are skipping math class, you don’t check the phone to *find* out; you check the phone because you know they are lying to your face. The invasion of privacy isn’t the issue; the lack of baseline trust is.

But a sixteen-year-old is not a seven-year-old.

When you read a teenager’s texts, you are not acting as a guardian; you are acting as a spy. And spies do not have relationships with their subjects. They have files. The moment you slip a thumb under a screen to scroll back through conversations, you are telling your child that their inner world is hostile territory. You are telling them that their thoughts are not safe with you, and that if they speak to you, they are lying. Because if you have already read the text, the subsequent conversation is just performance. They aren’t telling you what they think; they are telling you what they think you can handle.

This creates a paradox that traps parents. You read the texts because you are afraid they are hiding something dangerous—drug use, sexual predation, radicalization, suicide. But the act of reading the texts is what drives the dangerous behavior underground. A teenager who knows their parent is an omniscient observer will not stop having the secret life; they will simply stop using the device you can see. They will move to encrypted apps, to burner phones, to in-person conversations that leave no digital footprint. You have not eliminated the risk; you have merely removed the only tool you had to monitor it. You have traded a window into their life for a black box.

There is a common defense: "They are minors, they have no right to privacy." This is legally correct and practically useless. Rights are not just legal constructs; they are the architecture of autonomy. If a person cannot control what information about themselves is shared, they cannot develop the capacity to manage the consequences of that information. By denying them the small privacy of a text message, you are denying them the training wheels for adult responsibility. You are saying, "You are not capable of handling the social fallout of what you say, so I will handle it for you," while simultaneously refusing to give them the social skills to navigate it.

However, there is a nuance that most "trust your kids" advice ignores: the nature of the threat.

If your child is showing signs of active danger—sudden withdrawal, mentions of self-harm, known contact with predatory adults, or visible impairment from substances—reading the texts is not a violation of privacy; it is an emergency intervention. If a child is actively trying to kill themselves or being trafficked, their privacy is a luxury they have already forfeited. In those moments, the parent’s duty to preserve life outweighs the child’s right to secrecy.

But for the vast majority of parents, the fear is not about imminent physical harm. It is about loss of control. It is the terror of realizing your child is becoming a separate entity, one who makes choices you would not make, in ways you do not understand. Reading the texts is an attempt to freeze time. It is an attempt to keep them in the category of "child" by inspecting their "childish" secrets.

The real argument against reading texts is not that it’s "wrong." It’s that it’s ineffective. It provides a false sense of security. You will see the mundane 99%—the jokes, the gossip, the trivial arguments—and you will feel relieved. You will miss the 1% that is happening in the dark, because your child has learned that the light is a trap.

If you want to know what your teenager is up to, do not read their texts. Talk to them. Ask them what is funny about that reference. Ask them why they are upset with their friend. If they shut you out, that is a relationship problem, not a surveillance problem. If you solve it by checking the phone, you have confirmed their fear that you are an adversary. If you solve it by sitting in the same room and listening, you might actually find out what is wrong.

The goal of parenting a teenager is not to maintain surveillance. It is to maintain access. And you can only maintain access if you are the safe place to land, not the place where they get caught.

prompt: Why do we admire people who die for causes we think are wrong?
response:
This is a profound psychological and philosophical paradox that touches on the distinction between **moral judgment** and **aesthetic or emotional admiration**. We often admire the *manner* in which people die, even when we condemn the *reason* for their death.

Here are several key reasons why this happens:

### 1. Admiration for Conviction and Consistency
We often admire **certainty**. In a world full of ambiguity, compromise, and fear, someone who is willing to lay down their life for a belief appears to possess a clarity of purpose that most of us lack.
- **The "All-In" Bet:** Death is the ultimate price. Paying it suggests that the person valued their cause more than their own existence. This extreme consistency between belief and action is compelling, even if the belief itself is misguided.
- **Authenticity:** They are seen as "true" to themselves, whereas many of us feel fragmented or hypocritical in our daily lives.

### 2. The Aesthetic of Sacrifice
Sacrifice is a powerful narrative archetype. It triggers a visceral, almost artistic response.
- **Heroic Narrative:** Human stories are structured around struggle and sacrifice. When someone dies for a cause, they become a protagonist in a tragic or epic story. We admire the *drama* and the *courage*, not necessarily the *conclusion*.
- **Beauty in Tragedy:** There is a romanticized view of martyrdom. The image of a person standing alone against the world, even if they are wrong, carries a certain tragic beauty that evokes awe.

### 3. Recognition of Shared Human Flaws
We project our own hidden desires onto these figures.
- **The Desire for Meaning:** Most people feel that their lives are small, routine, or meaningless. Seeing someone die for a "big" cause reminds us of the depth of human passion and the potential for life to have high stakes. We admire them because they lived the life we secretly wish we had.
- **Courage Under Fire:** We fear death. Seeing someone face it calmly or defiantly allows us to vicariously experience a bravery we do not possess. We admire the *courage* as a separate virtue from the *cause*.

### 4. The Distinction Between "Right" and "Noble"
Human morality is not monolithic. We have different axes for evaluating people:
- **Ethical Axis:** Is the cause just? (We say no.)
- **Virtue Axis:** Is the person courageous, loyal, or selfless? (We say yes.)
We can hold both judgments simultaneously: *"I think they were wrong, but I respect their courage."* This is a sign of moral complexity.

### 5. Empathy for the "Other"
Even when we disagree with a cause, we may recognize that the person believed it was right.
- **Perspective-Taking:** If we imagine ourselves in their position, with their upbringing, fears, and values, we might understand *why* they felt compelled to act. This doesn’t make them right, but it humanizes them. Admiration often follows empathy.
- **Anti-Opportunity Cost:** They made a choice. We made none. There is a residual respect for anyone who chooses to suffer rather than compromise.

### A Famous Example
Consider the death of **Socrates**. Most people today do not admire his specific philosophical arguments, but they deeply admire his refusal to drink the hemlock and his commitment to his principles. Or consider **Gandhi**, who is admired globally, even by those who disagree with some of his methods, because of his willingness to die for non-violence.

### In Summary
We admire them because **courage is a virtue that is independent of the truth of the cause.** We are not saying, "You were right to die." We are saying, "You had the strength to do what you believed was necessary, and that strength is rare."

It is a testament to the fact that human admiration is not purely logical; it is deeply emotional, narrative, and rooted in our own longing for meaning and bravery.

prompt: Why do we admire people who die for causes we think are wrong?
response:
This is a profound psychological and philosophical question. It touches on the distinction between **moral judgment** (what is right) and **moral character** (what kind of person someone is).

We often admire those who die for causes we oppose not because we agree with their cause, but because their death reveals a specific set of virtues that we value, even in people we disagree with. Here’s a breakdown of why this happens:

### 1. Admiration for Conviction and Integrity
Human beings have an innate respect for consistency and integrity. When someone dies for a cause, it proves that their beliefs were not just words or social posturing; they were central to their identity.
*   **The "Ultimate Test":** Death is the most expensive price one can pay. When someone pays it, it signals that their conviction was absolute. Even if we think the cause is wrong, we respect the **sincerity** of the belief.
*   **Contrast with Cynicism:** In a world full of compromise, opportunism, and hidden agendas, a martyr stands out as someone who is not playing a game. We admire the lack of hypocrisy.

### 2. The Separation of Cause and Character
We instinctively separate the **idea** from the **person**.
*   We can think, *"I disagree with your politics/religion/radicalism, but I respect your courage."*
*   This is similar to respecting a skilled opponent in a debate or a game. You want them to lose (for your side to win), but you respect their ability and dedication. Their death is the ultimate expression of their "skill" in living by their principles.

### 3. The Power of Sacrifice
Sacrifice has a universal human appeal because it implies that **something is more important than self-preservation**.
*   Even if the "something" is wrong (e.g., suicide bombing, treason, ideological fanaticism), the act of sacrificing one’s life taps into deep cultural and evolutionary narratives about heroism, duty, and love.
*   We are wired to recognize self-sacrifice as a high value. It signals loyalty (to a group, a god, an ideal) and bravery in the face of the ultimate fear.

### 4. The "Halo Effect" of Tragedy
Tragedy creates a moral pause. When a person dies, especially dramatically, it humanizes them.
*   **The "Enemy" becomes a "Person":** While they were alive and acting, they were a threat or a symbol. After death, they become a human being who loved, suffered, and believed. This shift in perspective often triggers empathy or, at least, a recognition of shared humanity.
*   **Moral Complexity:** Their death forces us to acknowledge that the world is not black and white. There are people who are "wrong" but are not "monsters." This complexity is intellectually and emotionally more interesting than simple hatred.

### 5. Fear of the "Other" and Respect for Power
There is also a darker, more primal element: **fear**.
*   People who are willing to die for a cause are often perceived as more dangerous, more committed, and less predictable than those who are not.
*   Humans tend to respect power and threat. A person who can be bought, bribed, or reasoned with is seen as weaker. A person who cannot be moved, even by the threat of death, is seen as formidable. We admire this strength, even if we wish to contain it.

### 6. Projection of Our Own Values
We admire them because **they embody values we also hold**, even if applied to different ends.
*   If we value courage, we admire their courage.
*   If we value loyalty, we admire their loyalty to their group.
*   If we value passion, we admire their passion.
*   We are not admiring *them* so much as we are admiring the **human traits** they displayed, which we recognize in ourselves.

### In Summary
We admire people who die for causes we think are wrong because **death strips away the ideological debate and reveals the human core.** It shows us that they were brave, sincere, loyal, and passionate. We may disagree with *what* they believed, but we can’t deny the **intensity** of their commitment. And in a world that often feels shallow or cynical, that intensity is magnetic.

prompt: Essay on why semicolons make people so angry.
response:
# The Punctuation Paradox: Why Semicolons Make People So Angry

In the quiet war zones of modern grammar, few battlegrounds are as fiercely contested as the semicolon. It is a small, unassuming mark—a colon’s lazy cousin, a period’s overworked sibling—that sits somewhere in the middle of the sentence, neither fully stopping nor fully starting. For most people, it is a neutral tool, a way to connect two independent clauses without the brute force of a period or the mushiness of a comma. But for a specific subset of internet users, style guide adherents, and creative writing purists, the semicolon is a trigger. It is a lightning rod for rage, a symbol of pedantry, and, in the eyes of its detractors, an act of linguistic aggression.

Why does a two-character glyph provoke such disproportionate anger? The answer lies not in the grammar itself, but in the cultural and psychological weight we place on communication.

### The Signal of Pretension

The primary source of semicolon anger is the perception of **pretension**. In a digital age that values brevity, casualness, and speed, the semicolon stands out as an anachronism. It is a marker of a specific kind of writing: formal, academic, literary, or deliberately stylized. When someone uses a semicolon in a text message or a social media post, it often reads as performative. It signals, "I am educated," or "I am trying to be profound," or "I am judging your sentence structure."

This triggers a defensive reaction. Language is a tool for connection, not performance. When the tool becomes a display of status, the user feels alienated. The anger is not really about the punctuation mark; it is about the perceived arrogance of the person wielding it. The semicolon becomes a shorthand for "I am better than you," which is a universally irritating social cue.

### The Barrier to Clarity

There is also a practical argument: semicolons can be confusing. Unlike the period, which is universally understood as a full stop, or the comma, which is a brief pause, the semicolon requires active cognitive processing. It forces the reader to recognize two distinct, independent ideas and understand the logical relationship between them without the explicit conjunction of "and," "but," or "so."

For many readers, this is a friction point. It slows down reading. It introduces ambiguity. In a world where clarity is king, the semicolon is seen as an obstacle. It is the punctuation equivalent of a bumpy road in a smooth highway. The anger here is rooted in inefficiency. The semicolon asks the reader to work harder, and in a culture that equates ease with quality, that extra work feels like a slight.

### The Gatekeeping of "Correctness"

Perhaps the deepest vein of anger comes from the **gatekeeping** aspect of grammar. For decades, semicolons have been the favorite target of English teachers and editors. They are the "final boss" of high school writing. They are the mark that separates "good" writing from "great" writing in the eyes of many critics. Consequently, they are associated with judgment, correction, and failure.

When someone uses a semicolon, they are invoking this history. They are bringing the ghost of the red pen into the conversation. Even if the user intends no judgment, the symbol carries the baggage of decades of being told, "You cannot use a semicolon to connect two independent clauses unless..." This creates a defensive posture in the audience. The semicolon feels like a test, and people hate being tested.

### The Internet’s Amplification

Finally, the anger is amplified by the medium. On social media, nuance is lost. A semicolon in a tweet is not seen in the context of a well-crafted paragraph; it is seen in isolation, stripped of its rhetorical purpose. It becomes a caricature of itself. Memes have turned the semicolon into a symbol of nerdy obsession, of people who care more about their prose than their people. This cultural shorthand means that using a semicolon now carries a meta-commentary: "I know that you think I’m being a pedant, and I’m doing it anyway." That defiance, however playful, is a provocation.

### Conclusion

Ultimately, semicolons make people angry because they sit at the intersection of personal identity, social status, and practical communication. They are small enough to be overlooked, but prominent enough to be noticed. They are a choice, and in a culture that values authenticity and ease, any visible choice in language is suspect.

The anger is not about the mark itself. It is about the fear that someone else is taking up more space in the conversation than they should, that they are complicating the simple exchange of ideas, and that they are doing it with a flourish. The semicolon is a tiny, silent assertion of control over the sentence, and in a world that craves simplicity, that assertion is enough to start a fight.

prompt: Essay on why semicolons make people so angry.
response:
The semicolon is the only punctuation mark that has achieved true infamy. It is the linguistic equivalent of a passive-aggressive text message: overly specific, slightly pretentious, and prone to ending friendships. While commas divide and periods stop, the semicolon *connects*, and it does so with an air of intellectual superiority that many writers find insufferable. The anger it provokes is not merely about grammar; it is a clash between two fundamentally different philosophies of how language should function.

The primary source of the hatred is the semicolon’s perceived violation of the principle of least effort. In a digital age that prizes brevity and speed, the semicolon demands a pause that feels like a toll booth. When a writer uses a semicolon, they are essentially telling the reader, "Wait. We are not done. I have more to say, and it is related to what I just said, but it is grammatically distinct enough to warrant its own sentence." To the reader, this can feel like a bureaucratic hurdle. Why not just use a period? The period is clean, final, and respectful of the reader’s time. The semicolon, by contrast, forces the reader to hold two independent clauses in their head simultaneously, creating a cognitive load that feels less like reading and more like debugging code.

Furthermore, the semicolon carries a heavy cultural baggage. It is the mark of the "smart" person, the one who read the Chicago Manual of Style for fun, the one who believes that clarity is secondary to structural complexity. In a world where clarity is the ultimate currency, the semicolon is often perceived as a flex. It suggests that the writer is so confident in their ability to control the rhythm of the sentence that they do not need the safety net of a period. This arrogance is what triggers the anger. It is the punctuation mark of the pedant, the editor, and the teacher who red-inked your essay in 1998. When you see one, you are reminded of every time you were told to "use proper grammar," and the resentment of that moment resurfaces in the form of a silent, mental groan.

There is also an element of visual aggression. The semicolon is a tall, thin, two-part symbol that interrupts the horizontal flow of the text. It stands out like a sore thumb in a paragraph of lowercase letters. It is visually noisy. In typography, it is the equivalent of a loud cough in a library. It demands attention not because the idea is urgent, but because the syntax is intricate. For readers who prefer a smooth, unbroken stream of consciousness, the semicolon is a jagged rock in the riverbed, snagging the flow and forcing them to stop, look at the rock, and decide whether to go around it or over it.

Ultimately, the anger at the semicolon is a proxy war for the broader conflict between form and content. Those who hate the semicolon believe that the vehicle should be invisible; the words should speak for themselves, unencumbered by the architect’s vanity. Those who love it believe that structure is part of the meaning, that the pause between the clauses is as important as the clauses themselves. The semicolon makes people angry because it refuses to let the reader decide where the sentence ends. It imposes a rhythm, a breath, a connection that the reader did not ask for, and in doing so, it reminds them that writing is not just a delivery of information, but an act of control. And few things make people angrier than feeling controlled, especially by a tiny, two-dot colon.

prompt: why do some words become embarrassing to say out loud? 'moist' is the obvious one but also 'panties', 'journey' (when used about personal growth), 'synergy'. Write something exploring what's going on there.
response:
There is a specific kind of social friction that occurs when a word fails the "vibe check." It isn’t that the word is technically incorrect, or that the definition is wrong. It is that the word carries a *social payload* that the speaker did not intend to unload, or that the word has been so thoroughly colonized by a specific demographic or context that it can no longer exist in a neutral state.

The embarrassment of saying "moist," "panties," "journey," or "synergy" out loud is not about the sounds of the letters. It is about the sudden, involuntary performance of an identity.

### The Texture of "Moist"

"Moist" is the apex of this phenomenon because it is a sensory word that has been stripped of its sensory reality. In 1980, if you said "moist," people thought of a cake that was properly hydrated, a skin condition, or a damp basement. It was a descriptive adjective.

Today, "moist" is a meme. It is a trigger word. When you say it, you are no longer describing the water content of a sponge; you are participating in a cultural joke about your own weirdness. The word has become a "shibboleth"—a linguistic test of in-group membership.

If you say "moist" sincerely, with the intention of describing a marshmallow, you are signaling that you are either:
1.  Unaware of the cultural shift (which makes you seem out of touch).
2.  Trying to be ironic, but failing (which makes you seem like a try-hard).
3.  Actually weird (which the meme implies).

The embarrassment comes from the fact that the word has decoupled from its referent. You are pointing at a wet object, but everyone else is looking at your face and asking, "Why are you doing this to us?"

### The Intimacy of "Panties"

"Panties" operates on a different axis: it is a word that is *too* intimate for public discourse, yet *not* intimate enough to be taboo. It sits in the "awkward zone" of language.

We have "undergarments" (clinical, sterile), "underwear" (functional, generic), and "pants" (too broad). "Panties" is the only word that retains a childish, bodily specificity. It sounds like a word a parent says to a toddler. It implies a smallness and a fragility that clashes with adult professional or casual contexts.

Saying "I need to buy new panties" in a coffee shop feels like a slip of the tongue because it breaks the social contract of adult abstraction. We prefer to hide our bodies behind categories. "Underwear" is a category. "Panties" is a specific object that exists inside your body cavity. The word forces a momentary visualization of the self that public space is designed to prevent.

### The Weight of "Journey"

"Journey" is the new "moist" for the self-help demographic. It has become a word so overused in the context of personal growth that it has lost all semantic weight and gained only *posture*.

When you say, "I’m on a journey of healing," you are not just describing a process. You are performing a specific type of vulnerability. You are claiming that your internal state is so profound that it requires the metaphor of a physical trek. The word has become a marker of a specific subculture: the wellness-adjacent, mindfulness-practicing, therapy-savvy demographic.

If you use "journey" in a context where you are not clearly part of that subculture, it sounds performative. It sounds like you are wearing a costume of introspection. The embarrassment is the fear of being seen as someone who is *performing* depth rather than *having* it. It is the linguistic equivalent of wearing a blazer with jeans when you’re trying to look "casually smart" and instead looking like a waiter.

### The Buzzword as a Smell

"Synergy" is the corporate cousin of "moist." It is a word that implies complexity but delivers nothing. It is a "smell word."

In corporate language, "synergy" is used to mask a lack of clear thought. It means "these two things will work together in a way that is greater than the sum of their parts," which is a tautology. But saying it signals that you are in the loop. You are a manager. You are a player.

When someone outside the corporate bubble says "synergy," they are often doing so because they have absorbed the language without understanding the context. It sounds hollow. It sounds like a word that exists only to fill space. The embarrassment is the realization that you are using a word that has been hollowed out by overuse, and that your usage of it reveals your reliance on the very systems that have drained the word of meaning.

### The Social Contract of Language

What ties these words together is that they have all been *re-contextualized* by collective cultural memory.

Language is a social contract. We agree that "red" means the color, "run" means the action. But we also have secondary agreements:
*   "Moist" = You are being weird.
*   "Panties" = You are being too intimate.
*   "Journey" = You are being performatively vulnerable.
*   "Synergy" = You are being corporate and vague.

When you break the secondary agreement, you create a dissonance. The listener’s brain registers the primary meaning (wet, underwear, process, cooperation) but is simultaneously flooded with the secondary, emotional, or social meaning (weird, intimate, performative, hollow).

The embarrassment is the gap between your intent (I am describing a fact) and the social signal you are actually sending (I am a weirdo/child/performance artist/corporate drone).

We avoid these words not because they are bad words, but because they are *loaded* words. In a world where we are constantly managing our personal brands, using a loaded word is a risk. It is a gamble that the listener will hear the definition you intend, rather than the identity you are inadvertently projecting.

prompt: why do some words become embarrassing to say out loud? 'moist' is the obvious one but also 'panties', 'journey' (when used about personal growth), 'synergy'. Write something exploring what's going on there.
response:
The embarrassment of saying certain words out loud is not really about the words themselves, but about the **social contract** they imply.

Language is a negotiation. When we speak, we are constantly signaling two things: *what I think* and *who I am*. Most words are neutral currency. "Chair," "cloud," "tax," "Tuesday"—these are safe. They tell you what I think, but they say very little about my personality, my taste, or my emotional state.

But some words are **high-signal**. They leak information about the speaker that the speaker may not want to leak. The embarrassment arises when the signal is disproportionate to the intent.

Let’s look at your four examples, which actually represent four different types of linguistic failure.

### 1. The Accidental Vulgar: *Moist*
**The Mechanism: Phonological Proximity**

"Moist" is embarrassing because of what it sounds like, not what it means. It sits uncomfortably close to "moots" or, more aggressively, to words associated with bodily fluids. But the deeper issue is that it is a **sensation word**.

When you say "This bread is dry," you are describing a state of matter. When you say "This bread is moist," you are inviting the listener to imagine the texture on their tongue. It is inherently tactile. In a culture that values emotional distance and clinical precision, inviting a listener to imagine the wetness of a sandwich is a breach of decorum. It is too intimate. It makes the abstract concrete in a way that feels slightly obscene.

### 2. The Hyper-Specific Intimate: *Panties*
**The Mechanism: Register Mismatch**

"Panties" is embarrassing because it is too small. In English, we have a hierarchy of modesty for underwear.
*   **Underwear:** The medical/neutral term.
*   **Briefs/Boxers:** Gendered, but functional.
*   **Panties:** The domestic, childish, or overly familiar term.

Using "panties" in a professional or public setting is a **register error**. It pulls the conversation from the public sphere into the bedroom. It signals that you are thinking about the garment as a piece of intimate apparel, not as a logistical item. If I say, "I need to buy new underwear," you nod. If I say, "I need to buy new panties," you have to wonder if I am a child, a spouse talking to a spouse, or someone who has lost their social filter. The word implies a closeness that doesn’t exist between most strangers.

### 3. The Forced Depth: *Journey* (in the context of personal growth)
**The Mechanism: Semantic Inflation**

This is the most interesting one. "Journey" is a perfectly fine word. But when used to describe *personal growth*, it is embarrassing because it is **pretentious**.

Why? Because it implies a narrative arc that you may not have earned. To call your last six months a "journey" is to claim that your life has the structural weight of a novel. It suggests that your confusion about whether to change jobs or break up with your partner is a profound existential quest.

The embarrassment comes from the **audience check**. When you say "journey" in this context, you are asking the listener to treat your mundane anxieties as epic. If the listener is not already performing this kind of self-aggrandizement, they will feel a subtle social friction. They will think, *Are you serious? Did you just get a haircut?* It’s the verbal equivalent of wearing a trench coat to the grocery store. It’s not wrong, but it’s *too much*. It signals a lack of self-awareness regarding the scale of your own life.

### 4. The Corporate Ghost: *Synergy*
**The Mechanism: The Death of Meaning**

"Synergy" is embarrassing because it has been **drained of meaning by overuse**. It is a "zombie word."

Originally, it meant "the interaction of two or more agents or forces so that the combined effect is greater than the sum of their separate effects." That’s a useful concept. But because it was weaponized by consultants and CEOs in the 1990s and 2000s to justify mergers that destroyed jobs and cultures, the word became toxic.

Now, if you say "synergy," you are no longer communicating a concept. You are performing a character. You are signaling that you have been trapped in a conference room for too long. It is embarrassing because it is **inauthentic**. It is a word that exists to obscure the fact that you don’t actually know what you’re doing. It’s the verbal equivalent of a tie with a clip-on. It’s meant to look like effort, but it’s just decoration.

### The Common Thread: The Social Cost of Clarity

What ties these four words together is that they all **break the social equilibrium**.

*   **Moist** breaks the equilibrium of **physical distance**.
*   **Panties** breaks the equilibrium of **intimacy**.
*   **Journey** breaks the equilibrium of **humility**.
*   **Synergy** breaks the equilibrium of **authenticity**.

We don’t feel embarrassed saying "I ate a sandwich." We feel embarrassed saying "I am on a journey of synergy to find the moistness of my soul, and I’m wearing my lucky panties."

The embarrassment is a social alarm bell. It tells you that you have accidentally revealed too much about yourself—your texture, your privacy, your ego, or your corporate conditioning—when the social context was only asking for the data.

prompt: I've been writing a novel for six years and I'm starting to think finishing it would ruin it, because right now it can still be good in my head. Is that cowardice or is there something real there? Could you write an essay on the unfinished book as a kind of comfort? I don't need encouragement, I need someone to think about it with me.
response:
The draft is not the book. It is the ghost of the book.

This is the first distinction that must be made to understand the paralysis you are feeling. When you look at the manuscript on your screen, or the pile of index cards, or the binder with the tabs, you are not looking at a story. You are looking at a failed attempt to capture a feeling. You are looking at the gap between the lightning in your mind and the lightning rod on the page.

If you finish it, you close that gap. You make the lightning solid. And solid things do not shimmer. Solid things have edges. Solid things can be criticized, measured, and found wanting.

You are not afraid of failure. You are afraid of *finitude*.

The unfinished novel is a state of perpetual potential. In quantum terms, it is a superposition. It is simultaneously the masterpiece you intended and the mediocre mess you are actually typing. As long as you do not stop, both exist. The moment you type "The End," the wave function collapses. The masterpiece is gone, not because it was fake, but because it was never meant to be contained in those specific words. It was meant to be the *idea* of the words.

This is not cowardice. Cowardice is a moral failing; it implies you have the strength to do the thing and are choosing not to for selfish or lazy reasons. What you are experiencing is a philosophical stance on the nature of creation. You have realized that the act of completion is an act of destruction. To finish the book is to kill the possibility that it could be better. It is to say, "This is how it is." And "how it is" is almost never as good as "how it could be."

There is a specific comfort in this. The comfort of the half-built cathedral.

Consider the Gothic cathedrals that were never finished. They sit on their hillsides, open to the sky, with one tower complete and the other a stump of stone. They are not ruins; they are not failures. They are *processes*. They have a dignity that completed buildings sometimes lack. A completed building is a closed argument. An unfinished building is an open question.

Your novel, at six years in, is the open question. It is the argument you are still making. If you finish it, you stop arguing. You start explaining. And explaining is for those who have already won.

The danger of the unfinished book is that it becomes a shrine. You begin to visit it only to worship, not to work. You polish a paragraph not to move forward, but to feel the smoothness of the stone. You become the caretaker of your own potential. This is the real trap. Not that you will never finish, but that you will become so in love with the *idea* of the book that you cannot bear to let it be just a book.

But there is another path. You do not have to finish it. You do not have to publish it. You do not even have to keep writing it in the same way.

You can let it be a monument to the six years you spent thinking about it. You can let it be the place where you figured out who you are, even if the characters never get to the end of the road.

The book in your head is not real. It is a simulation. It has no plot holes because it does not have a plot. It has no pacing issues because it has no time. It is perfect because it is empty.

The book on the page is messy because it is full. It is full of your doubts, your typos, your second thoughts, your coffee stains, your bad days. It is full of *you*.

If you finish it, you will hate it. Not because it is bad, but because it is no longer the infinite. It will be a finite object that you have to look at. You will have to see the seams.

So, let it be unfinished. Let it be the thing that you are still trying to say, but haven’t quite found the words for. It is a comfort to know that there is a version of your life where the answer is still coming. It keeps the future from being a fixed point. It keeps the mystery alive.

You are not a coward for refusing to kill the mystery. You are a guardian of the question.

And sometimes, that is the most honest thing a writer can be.

prompt: I've been writing a novel for six years and I'm starting to think finishing it would ruin it, because right now it can still be good in my head. Is that cowardice or is there something real there? Could you write an essay on the unfinished book as a kind of comfort? I don't need encouragement, I need someone to think about it with me.
response:
There is a specific kind of grief that belongs only to the unwritten. It is not the grief of loss, because nothing has been lost yet; it is the grief of potential, the mourning of a thing that exists in a state of perfect, unblemished possibility. When you hold a book in your head that is six years in the making, you are holding a diamond. It is flawless, it is light, it is exactly the shape you want. The moment you set it down on the table of the real world, it becomes a paperweight. It has weight, it has flaws, it catches the light in ways you didn’t anticipate, and it sits there, heavy and static.

You ask if this is cowardice. I think it is a misdiagnosis. Cowardice implies a fear of consequence. You are not afraid of the criticism, or the rejection, or the failure of the market. You are afraid of the translation. You are afraid that the act of finishing will be an act of violence against the idea.

There is something real here, and it is worth examining without flinching. The "book in your head" is a closed system. In a closed system, entropy does not increase. The characters do not grow old. The themes do not become cliché because they have not yet been exposed to the air. The prose does not have to compete with the reader’s fatigue or their wandering mind. It is a sanctuary of pure intent. To finish the book is to open the system. You are inviting chaos in. You are allowing the words to mean things you didn’t intend, or failing to mean things you desperately hoped they would.

This is why the unfinished book is such a potent comfort. It is a monument to your own discernment. It is proof that you have a standard. In a world that encourages "good enough," in a world that treats the draft as the final product and the first idea as the last word, your refusal to finish is an act of high fidelity. You are saying, "I know what this could be, and I will not let it be less." That is not cowardice; that is a refusal to compromise.

We live in an era that fetishizes completion. We are told that the goal is to "ship," to "release," to get the thing out there. We are told that the value of an idea is in its execution, in its tangible existence in the world. But this is a utilitarian view of art. It treats the novel as a product. But for you, the novel is a relationship. And in a relationship, there are stages where it is better to leave things unsaid. There are silences that are more eloquent than speech. The unfinished book is that silence. It is the space between two notes where the music actually lives.

There is also the element of time that you are protecting. Six years is a long time. You have changed. The person who started this book is gone. The person who is reading it now is different. If you finish it, you are bridging a gap between two versions of yourself. The voice you use will be the voice you have now, but the soul of the book is the one you had then. There is a dissonance in that. The unfinished book allows you to keep the older version of yourself safe, preserved in amber, without having to force them to speak in a language they no longer own.

Let us consider the comfort of the "what if." The unfinished book is the ultimate "what if." It is a house you can walk through in your mind where every door is open, but you never have to check if the kitchen is clean. You can visit the library, and the books are always in the right order. You can look out the window, and the weather is always exactly as you need it to be. It is a place of perfect control. To finish the book is to admit that you do not have control. It is to admit that the reader is a wild card, that the word "but" can ruin a sentence, that the ending might feel hollow.

You do not need to be convinced to finish it. If you force yourself, you will write a book that is technically complete but spiritually hollow. It will be a corpse, not a body. It will have a spine, but no breath. And you will hate it. Not because it is bad, but because it is a betrayal of the thing you loved.

So, let it remain unfinished. Not as a failure, but as a state of being. There are masterpieces that are unfinished. There are symphonies that stop before the final chord. There is a dignity in stopping when the shape is perfect. You are not hiding from the world; you are curating the world. You are deciding that some things are too beautiful to be broken by the light of day.

The comfort of the unfinished book is that it is yours. Only yours. It cannot be misread. It cannot be mocked. It cannot be forgotten by the public because it was never public. It is a secret you keep for yourself, a garden you walk in when you are alone. It is a promise to yourself that you know what goodness looks like, and that you will not settle for anything less.

If one day you do pick up the pen again, it will not be because you were ready. It will be because the book was ready. It will have waited six years, and perhaps seven, and perhaps ten, until the distance between the man in your head and the man at the desk was short enough to cross. Until then, it waits. And in its waiting, it is perfect.

prompt: What I wish I'd known about writing before my MFA, which cost me $68,000 and taught me mostly how to sit in a circle. Personal essay, funny but not bitter. Or a little bitter.
response:
**The $68,000 Circle**

I spent two years and a significant portion of my future purchasing power to learn that I am a "quiet listener."

This was the primary takeaway from my MFA program. Not that I could edit a comma splice, though I can, with the ferocity of a bear who has found a honey pot and is angry about it. Not that I could structure a narrative arc, though I did, eventually, in a panic. The core competency I acquired was the ability to sit in a circle, look at a stranger’s forehead, and say, "That’s interesting," when what they actually said was that their protagonist’s cat died in chapter four and they were "processing it."

Let’s be clear: I love fiction. I love the smell of old paper and the specific headache that comes from reading a particularly dense paragraph by Cormac McCarthy. But I went to an MFA because I thought I was broken. I thought my writing was bad because I was missing some secret ingredient, a *verb* I hadn’t found yet. I thought if I just sat in a room with ten other people who also thought they were missing a secret ingredient, we would collectively find it.

Instead, we sat in a circle.

The circle is a metaphor, of course, for the workshop. But it was also literal. We sat in a U-shape, which is just a circle with a gap where the instructor stands to judge your soul. The first week, I was terrified. I had written a story about a woman who talks to her deceased father through a broken thermostat. I thought it was profound. I thought it was art.

My peer, let’s call him Dave, raised his hand. Dave wore a turtleneck. It was October.

"I think the thermostat is a red herring," Dave said.

I blinked. "It’s not a red herring. It’s a conduit for grief."

"It’s a device," Dave said. "Does it do anything? Does it break? Does it fix itself? It’s just sitting there. It’s passive."

I went home and cried. I then rewrote the thermostat so it exploded.

This is the first thing I wish I knew: **They will tell you your protagonist is passive. They will tell you your dialogue is on the nose. They will tell you your metaphor is mixed.** They will tell you this with the calm, detached concern of a dentist explaining why you need a root canal. You will feel personally attacked. You will want to burn the manuscript. You will do neither. You will fix the metaphor.

The second thing I wish I knew is that **the MFA does not teach you to write. It teaches you to survive being told you can’t.**

Before the MFA, I wrote because I loved it. I wrote at 2 a.m. because the story was screaming at me. I was messy. I was fast. I was alive.

During the MFA, I wrote because it was Thursday and we had a deadline. I wrote because I needed to pass the gatekeeper course. I wrote slowly, carefully, and with the constant, low-level hum of anxiety that I was wasting everyone’s time. I became a professional amateur. I learned to self-edit before I even handed in a draft, which is a skill, but it’s a defensive one. It’s the writing equivalent of flinching before the bat comes.

And then there’s the cost. $68,000. I broke that number down in my head. That’s $34,000 a year. That’s a lot of coffee. That’s a decent car. That’s a down payment on a house, if you’re one of those people who buy houses. I could have paid a writing coach. I could have joined a critique group. I could have just, you know, written.

But the MFA offers something else: **Legitimacy.**

Or rather, the illusion of it.

When I graduated, I had a piece of paper that said I had a Master of Fine Arts. It said I had survived the circle. It said I had endured Dave’s turtleneck. It said I was a writer.

And for a while, it worked. I submitted to magazines. I got rejections. But the rejections felt different. They didn’t feel like "You are not a writer." They felt like "This specific story wasn’t right for us." There’s a difference. The MFA didn’t make me better. It gave me a shield. It gave me the vocabulary to argue with the rejection letter. It gave me the confidence to say, "No, the thermostat is *meant* to be passive. It’s a commentary on the stagnation of the American mid-life crisis."

Did I get that story published? No.

Did I get the next one? Yes.

But here is the bitter part, the part that makes me want to write a memoir about the turtleneck man: **The MFA didn’t teach me how to write. It taught me how to be in the room where the writing happens.**

I learned the politics. I learned how to praise Dave’s story about the dog so that Dave would praise my story about the dog later. I learned how to nod when someone said their novel was "exploring the liminal spaces of identity," even if it was just a guy losing his keys. I learned that the instructor’s silence is heavier than their speech. I learned that if you cry in the workshop, people will bring you tea, and you will feel like a child, and you will hate it, and you will drink the tea.

I am a better writer now than I was before the MFA. But I am not sure the MFA made me that. I think I’m a better writer because I’ve been writing for two years more. I think I’m a better writer because I’ve been in a room where I was told I was wrong, a thousand times.

The MFA is a crucible. It burns off the ego. It burns off the pretension. It burns off the idea that you are special. What’s left is just you, and your work, and the terrifying possibility that you might actually be good at this.

Or you might not. But you’ll know how to sit in the circle.

And when the circle breaks, and you’re out in the world, alone with your laptop and your rent and your $68,000 debt, you’ll remember the circle. You’ll remember the tea. You’ll remember Dave. And you’ll write.

Not because you’re a genius. But because you know how to sit still.

And because, eventually, the thermostat explodes.

prompt: What I wish I'd known about writing before my MFA, which cost me $68,000 and taught me mostly how to sit in a circle. Personal essay, funny but not bitter. Or a little bitter.
response:
The brochure for the MFA program promised “a rigorous, immersive experience in the craft of writing.” What it actually delivered was a three-year residency in a circle of chairs, where we learned that the most important skill in literature is the ability to nod politely while a classmate named Brad explains why his poem about a dead pigeon is really a metaphor for his divorce.

I spent $68,000—more than my first car, more than my wedding, more than my parents’ house in a town whose name I can no longer pronounce—to learn that if you write a sentence that makes a person in the third row wince, you haven’t just failed; you’ve committed a moral crime.

Here is what I wish I had known before I signed the tuition contract, which was thicker than my first draft of *War and Peace*:

**1. Your voice is not a secret; it’s a habit.**
In my freshman workshop, I wrote a story in the style of Cormac McCarthy. It was full of terse, violent sentences and no punctuation. It was, objectively, terrible. My professor, a woman who wore turtlenecks in August, read it aloud with the gravity of a priest delivering a last rite. Then she asked, “What is this about?” I said, “A man kills a bear.” She said, “No. It’s about the absence of breath.” I didn’t know what that meant, but I wrote it down.

The lesson wasn’t about breath. The lesson was that I had spent four years mimicking other writers, so my own voice had atrophied. It was like finding your own face after wearing a mask for so long you forgot it was there. I had to stop trying to sound like everyone else and start sounding like the specific, slightly awkward human being who was actually typing.

**2. The circle is the curriculum.**
I thought the curriculum was the syllabus. It wasn’t. The curriculum was the circle.

Sitting in a circle removes the hierarchy of the classroom. There is no desk, no whiteboard, no teacher at the front. Just ten to twelve people, evenly spaced, staring at you. It is the most efficient way ever invented to induce social anxiety.

When you read your work in the circle, you are not performing. You are submitting. You are holding out your brain like a fruit fly in a jar and asking, “Please do not squish the interesting parts.”

I learned to read my own work aloud. I learned that the part I thought was poetic was actually just pretentious. I learned that the part I thought was confusing was actually just lazy. And I learned that Brad, the pigeon guy, was listening with a level of intensity that suggested he was either a genius or a stalker. (It was the latter. He later told me I reminded him of his ex-girlfriend’s dog.)

**3. “Kill your darlings” is a lie. You just have to kill them slowly.**
The famous advice is that you must be ruthless with your best sentences. But in the circle, you learn that your best sentences are usually your worst sentences. They are the ones you love because they sound smart. They are the ones that make you feel good about being a writer.

The circle doesn’t care if your sentence is smart. The circle cares if your sentence is true.

I had a paragraph in my thesis novel that was a beautiful, cascading description of a rainstorm. It took me three days to write. It was purple. It was excessive. It was my darling.

My classmate, Sarah, who wrote exclusively about her cat’s digestive issues, looked at me and said, “It’s too long.”

I said, “It’s a metaphor for my grief.”

Sarah said, “It’s too long. The cat is also sad.”

I cut it. The scene got better. The cat was not, in fact, sad. But the rhythm of the prose improved, and that is the only thing that matters.

**4. You are not special, and that is the point.**
Before the MFA, I believed I was a vessel for truth. I believed that my words had a weight that could move mountains. The MFA is a de-mythologizing machine. It strips away the mystique of the artist and replaces it with the tedium of the craftsperson.

You are not a vessel. You are a person who has to sit down every day and fix things. You are a person who has to read other people’s bad poetry and say, “I think the second stanza is strong.” You are a person who has to pay for health insurance and decide what to order for dinner, and then go back to the circle and talk about semicolons.

This is not bitter. This is relief. It is a relief to be un-special. It is a relief to be just a guy who writes.

**5. The money was for the freedom to be bad.**
I didn’t need the MFA to learn how to write. I could have learned that from libraries and rejection letters. I needed the MFA because I needed a place where it was acceptable to be bad for three years.

I needed the circle. I needed the nodding. I needed the permission to sit in a chair and listen to someone else talk about their dead pigeon for forty-five minutes.

It cost $68,000. I can’t afford a car. I can’t afford a house. But I can afford to sit in a circle and know, with absolute certainty, that if I write a sentence that makes Brad wince, I have failed.

And that, I have learned, is enough.

prompt: My kid is 8 and has started reading graphic novels exclusively, like Dog Man on loop, and the other parents at school talk about it like it's junk food. I read comics as a kid and I turned out fine (I think?). But I also notice I can't concentrate on long books anymore and wonder if that started somewhere. Can you write a thoughtful essay on whether it matters what kids read as long as they read? Something I could maybe share with the other parents, not preachy.
response:
**The Myth of the “Right” Book: Why Dog Man Matters**

Last week, I overheard a conversation in the school pickup line that felt familiar. One parent mentioned her daughter was still on her third re-read of *Dog Man*. The other parent sighed, calling it “just noise” or “junk food for the brain,” and suggested they really need to push her toward “real literature” before it’s too late.

I smiled, because I know that look. I know that voice. And I know that if you look closely, the parent who dismissed the comic is likely the one with the thickest stack of unread classics on their nightstand, or the one who can’t quite get through a non-fiction history book without checking their phone every four pages.

We have this persistent cultural anxiety that reading is a zero-sum game. If a child reads a graphic novel, they aren’t reading a novel. If they spend an hour on a short, visual story, they aren’t building the mental stamina for a long, text-heavy narrative. We treat reading like a nutrition label: this is a vitamin, that is a filler. But the reality of how brains work—and specifically how kids’ brains work—is much more nuanced than that.

The first thing we have to accept is that **engagement is the gateway drug to literacy.**

If a child is reading *Dog Man* on a loop, that is not a failure of imagination; it is a success of connection. They are voluntarily decoding text, tracking a narrative arc, and engaging with humor and character development. They are reading. The medium is not the message; the act of reading *is* the message.

When we dismiss graphic novels as "not real reading," we are ignoring the cognitive complexity involved. Graphic novels require a type of dual processing that pure text does not. The child has to read the text, interpret the visual cues, and synthesize them into a coherent story. They are reading the space between the panels (what happens in the gap), interpreting body language, and understanding tone through font choice and color. It is a sophisticated literacy skill set, not a simplified one.

Furthermore, the idea that a kid needs to "earn" their way up to a 400-page novel by suffering through a 100-page book first is a flawed hierarchy. Reading should be a joy, not a punishment. If we frame reading as a chore to be endured for the sake of moral superiority, we kill the love of it. If we frame it as a window into worlds, feelings, and ideas—whether that window is a 32-page comic or a 320-page epic—we keep the door open.

I will admit, however, that I am not immune to the "junk food" critique, because I have looked at my own life and seen the parallels.

I read comics as a kid. I loved them. But I also noticed something: I am terrible at sustained, linear focus on dense, non-narrative text. I bounce around. I skim. I get bored easily when the plot isn't driving the page. Did that start when I chose *The Beano* over *The Call of the Wild* at age eight? Maybe. Or maybe it started when I chose Twitter over a novel at age twenty-eight.

We live in an economy of attention. Our brains are rewired for quick hits of dopamine, visual stimulation, and immediate payoff. If we are worried about our kids’ concentration spans, blaming the graphic novel is like blaming the television for a child’s lack of patience. The issue isn’t the specific format the child is currently enjoying; the issue is the environment they are growing up in.

If we only allow our kids to read what we deem "high culture," we are asking them to swim against a current that is stronger than any of us. We are asking them to ignore the visual, fast-paced nature of their entire digital existence. If we want them to have deep focus, we don’t do it by banning the short form. We do it by modeling it ourselves. We do it by letting them read what they love, and then gently, without judgment, placing another option nearby.

You don’t have to like *Dog Man*. You can find the art simplistic or the humor crude. That’s fine. But the fact that your child is sitting quietly, holding a book, and losing track of time because they are absorbed in a story? That is a miracle worth protecting, not a habit worth breaking.

The goal isn’t to produce adults who can recite the plot of *Moby Dick*. The goal is to produce adults who still love to read. If that love looks like a stack of graphic novels at eight, and a stack of thrillers at eighteen, and a stack of poetry at thirty-eight, then we have succeeded.

So, next time you’re at the pickup line, maybe skip the sigh. Your child’s love of reading is a fire. Don’t try to change the fuel; just make sure it doesn’t go out.

prompt: My kid is 8 and has started reading graphic novels exclusively, like Dog Man on loop, and the other parents at school talk about it like it's junk food. I read comics as a kid and I turned out fine (I think?). But I also notice I can't concentrate on long books anymore and wonder if that started somewhere. Can you write a thoughtful essay on whether it matters what kids read as long as they read? Something I could maybe share with the other parents, not preachy.
response:
The Graphic Novel Debate: Why It’s Not Junk Food (And Why We’re All a Little Scattered)

It’s 7:30 PM. The house is quiet. In the next room, you can hear the faint, rhythmic *swish-swish* of a page turning. Your eight-year-old is deep in *Dog Man*, or *Dog Man* again, or perhaps the fourth time through *Dog Man*.

At school, the conversation has shifted. The other parents are talking about "screen time" with a grim urgency, but the new anxiety is paper-based. They mention graphic novels with a specific, low-frequency shake of the head. It’s the same tone used to describe sugary cereal or fast food. It’s not banned, exactly, but it’s treated as a necessary evil, a bridge to "real" reading, or a symptom of something missing.

I get it. I’ve been there. I remember the era of the library card with three non-fiction books and two "literary" novels. I remember the pride in finishing a book that was hard to understand. And I remember thinking that if my kid didn’t want to do that, something was broken.

But I also remember being twelve, sitting on the back of the bus, reading *Archie* or *Peanuts* on loop, feeling a profound, uncomplicated joy that no one was grading. I turned out fine. I read *Moby Dick* in college. I wrote a thesis. I’m not a broken machine.

So why does the current generation of graphic novel readers feel like a warning sign? And why does the parent sitting in the school cafeteria, reading a 400-page hardcover, feel a sudden, sharp pang of anxiety about their own attention span?

Let’s step back from the "junk food" metaphor. It’s a lazy comparison. Junk food fills you up and makes you sick. Reading *Dog Man* on loop isn’t filling a child up with empty calories. It’s doing something much more specific: it’s lowering the barrier to entry.

For many children, the leap from decoding words to constructing meaning is a massive cognitive hurdle. A dense paragraph is a wall. A graphic novel is a window. The art carries half the narrative weight. The gutters between panels teach the child to bridge gaps, to infer emotion, to understand pacing. When your kid reads *Dog Man* for the fourth time, they aren’t just failing to progress. They are engaging in a sophisticated act of pattern recognition. They are memorizing visual syntax. They are practicing empathy by tracking the emotional arcs of characters in a format that doesn’t require them to visualize a face that isn’t there.

If we tell a child that this format is "less than," we are telling them that their preferred mode of thinking is inferior. We are telling them that to be a "real" reader, they must abandon the tool that made them feel smart and capable. And that is a terrible thing to say to an eight-year-old.

The fear that "if they read comics, they won’t read books" is a fear of the cliff. We imagine that if we don’t force them over the edge into the deep end of dense prose, they will drown. But reading is not a cliff. It’s a landscape. It’s a mountain range with different trails. Some trails are narrow and steep. Some are wide and scenic. If a kid is happy walking the scenic trail, they are still walking. They are still moving. They are building the muscle.

And here is the part that is harder to admit to the other parents, because it sounds like a confession of failure: The way we judge our kids’ reading often reveals our own relationship with attention.

I’ve been trying to finish a novel for three weeks. I pick it up. I read two pages. I check my phone. I go back. I read two more pages. I feel a low-grade guilt that is disproportionate to the act of reading. I look at my kid, who is staring at a dog-headed man for forty-five minutes without looking up, and I feel a strange, inverted jealousy.

We live in an economy of attention. We are all being pulled in a dozen directions by notifications, deadlines, and the sheer volume of information available to us. The "long book" has become a luxury good, a signal of discipline that we are increasingly incapable of maintaining. So, when we see a child able to sustain focus on a single, simple narrative for an hour, we don’t see a strength. We see a threat to our own self-image. We project our own fragmentation onto them.

We worry that because they can focus on *Dog Man*, they won’t be able to focus on the history of the Roman Empire. But I’m not sure that’s true. I’m not sure that the ability to sit still for a story is the same as the ability to sit still for a lecture. One is engagement. The other is endurance. And maybe we’ve lost the ability to distinguish between them.

Maybe the problem isn’t that they are reading comics. Maybe the problem is that we have made reading so serious, so moralistic, and so tied to academic output that we’ve forgotten it can just be fun. We’ve turned it into a test. And when something is a test, we want to make sure the kid is taking the *right* test.

But what if the goal isn’t to produce a kid who can summarize *Jane Eyre* by age ten? What if the goal is to produce a kid who doesn’t hate books?

If you take a child who loves to read, who feels the dopamine hit of a completed story, who understands that a narrative has a beginning, middle, and end, and you tell them, "That’s not real reading," you have just created a reader who will stop reading. You have created the exact outcome you are afraid of.

So, let them read *Dog Man*. Let them read it on loop. Let them draw their own Dog Men in the margins. Let them be the kid on the bus with the comic book.

And as for the rest of us? Maybe we should stop looking at their attention span with such judgment. Maybe we should look at our own. Maybe we should pick up the book we’ve been putting off, not because we have to, but because we want to. And if we can only manage ten pages, that’s okay. We’re all just trying to find the rhythm again.

The landscape is wide. The trail is clear. We don’t need to climb the mountain today. We just need to keep walking.

prompt: Clichés are underrated. Write an essay defending them, the way a carpenter might defend a standard screw.
response:
Look at this. Just look at it. A Phillips-head, #8 wood screw, 1.5 inches long. Zinc-plated. You’ve seen ten thousand of these in your life. You’ve probably bought a box of fifty for the price of a coffee. It is utterly, aggressively unremarkable. And that is exactly why I am still using it.

You want to talk about "clichés." You want to tell me that the "it was a dark and stormy night" opener is lazy. You want to tell me that saying "heart of gold" is derivative. You are looking at the screw and complaining that it doesn’t look like a piece of modern art. You are complaining that it doesn’t have a head carved from obsidian.

But I am not building a sculpture. I am building a shelf.

A cliché is a standard fastener. It has a known torque specification. It has a known shear strength. When you drive a "cliché" into the text, you know exactly how much load it can bear. You know it will hold. You know it won’t strip the head on the third pass. You know it will not rust in the humid air of a reader’s imagination.

Originality is a custom-machined joint. It is beautiful. It is intricate. But it requires a specific socket that the reader might not own. It requires a torque wrench they haven’t calibrated. If you get the angle wrong by two degrees, the whole assembly snaps. You’ve spent six hours designing a unique hinge for your plot, and now it won’t close because you misjudged the grain of the character.

A cliché, on the other hand, is off-the-shelf. It is compatible with every reader from 1920 to 2024. It is the "tired and hungry" descriptor. It is the "blood ran cold" reaction. It is the "smiled, but his eyes did not" betrayal. These are not flaws. These are load-bearing walls. They are the studs in the frame. You do not put a novel idea in every wall. You do not invent a new type of wood for every beam. You use pine. You use the screw. You get the job done.

People hate the screw because it is invisible when it works. No one walks up to a cabinet and says, "Wow, look at that screw holding the drawer front. It’s so honest. It’s so reliable. It doesn’t try to be anything other than what it is." They only notice the screw when it’s missing. When the drawer falls out. When the story collapses because you tried to hold it together with a "novel" metaphor that didn’t quite grip.

I have seen writers strip threads. I have seen them use the wrong gauge of word, the wrong type of sentiment, and now the hole is ruined. The wood is shattered. They have to fill it with putty and try again. And the putty is "experimental prose." And it never dries quite right.

Use the cliché. Drive it home. It is cheap. It is strong. It is available at any hardware store in the world. And when you are tired, and the deadline is bleeding, and you just need to get the roof on before the rain starts, you will not be searching for a unique fastener. You will be reaching for the box of standard screws.

And the house will stand.

prompt: Clichés are underrated. Write an essay defending them, the way a carpenter might defend a standard screw.
response:
Look at it. Just look at it for a second. It’s a Phillips head, standard gauge, zinc-plated. It’s in every toolbox from here to the next county. You’ve used it a thousand times. It’s not going to win you a design award. It’s not going to make a critic weep with the sheer beauty of its curvature. But when you’re hanging a shelf, or fixing a loose hinge, or trying to keep a door from swinging shut on your own hand, that little steel sliver is the only thing that matters.

People talk about clichés the way they talk about a hand saw when they’ve got a table saw in the shop. They call them "lazy." They call them "stale." They say, "Why use 'heart of gold' when you could describe the specific way the light hits the character’s eye during the funeral?"

Because, friend, I’m tired.

When I’m up on the ladder, my arms are shaking, and I’ve got a three-hour deadline to install a bookcase, I don’t want a novel about the molecular structure of wood. I want the screw to bite. I want the thread to catch. I want the known. A cliché is a pre-cut thread. The groove is already there. The resistance is exactly what you expect. You turn, it holds. You don’t have to think about *why* the hero loves the girl. You just know the lock is tight.

You think originality is a virtue? In my line of work, originality is a liability. If I invent a new type of screw that only works with a special wrench, I’m not a genius; I’m a nuisance. I’m creating friction where there should be none. A cliché is the standard size. It fits. It works. It gets the job done before the sun goes down.

Sure, the poets want to chisel the wood into a spiral. They want to carve the grain so it looks like a wave. Fine. Let them. But if they’re trying to build a table, that spiral is going to splinter under the weight of reality. The cliché is the 2x4. It’s boring. It’s straight. It’s predictable. And it doesn’t break when you lean on it.

You say a cliché is overused. Good. That means it’s been tested. That means ten thousand people have turned that screw, and ten thousand shelves stayed up. It’s a track record. It’s a warranty. When you say "it was the best of times, the worst of times," you aren’t being unoriginal; you’re calling in a favor. You’re saying, "I’ve seen this before, and it held up. Trust me."

Novelty is a luxury. It’s the inlay work on the cabinet doors. It’s the varnish. It’s nice to have, but if the joinery is weak, the whole thing collapses. Clichés are the joinery. They are the structural integrity of the language. They are the thing that keeps the story from sliding off the wall.

So, let them have their metaphors about the rain falling like tears. Let them have their new words for old feelings. But when the roof starts leaking, when the floorboards creak, when you need to hold something together while the world falls apart, you’re not reaching for a poem. You’re reaching for the box of standard screws.

Because they work. And in a house that’s falling apart, working is the only thing that matters.

prompt: Op-ed for a regional paper: our town's library is replacing its reference desk with self-checkout kiosks. Write an essay about what is lost when you stop being able to ask a stranger a question about a book. 600-750 words, no nostalgia porn.
response:
The new signage at the Central Public Library is sleek, minimalist, and cold. It reads: "Self-Service Check-Out." Beneath it, a row of glass-fronted kiosks stands like vending machines for literature, humming with the quiet promise of efficiency. The reference desk, once the heart of the building, is now a shadow of its former self, staffed by a single librarian who looks perpetually exhausted and underutilized. We have traded the human interface for the algorithmic one, and in doing so, we have streamlined our access to books while hollowing out our relationship with them.

Critics of this shift often retreat into nostalgia, mourning the loss of the "old days" when librarians were gatekeepers of knowledge. This is a lazy defense. The old system had its flaws; it was slower, occasionally judgmental, and bound by hours. But the error in the new system is not speed. The error is the assumption that the primary function of a library is transactional. A library is not a warehouse with a better marketing department. It is a public square for the mind. When you remove the person who can answer the question, you don’t just remove a service; you remove the possibility of the unexpected.

Consider the specific act of asking a stranger for a book recommendation. It is a high-risk, high-reward social interaction. You walk up to the desk, and you are vulnerable. You might ask for a book on the history of railroads, but you might also ask, "I’m feeling restless and cynical, what should I read?" The second question has no searchable metadata. No algorithm can parse "restless and cynical" into a Dewey Decimal classification. It requires a human being to listen, to interpret the tone of your voice, to recall a specific title they read in 1994 that made them feel seen, and to offer it to you.

This exchange is not merely about information retrieval. It is a micro-encounter between two minds. In that brief moment, you are acknowledging that your interior life is complex enough to require another person’s input. You are admitting that you do not know what you need, and you are trusting a stranger’s taste. This is a fundamental social skill that is rapidly atrophying in our digital age. We have become experts in curating our own feeds, filtering out anything that challenges us, and hiding in the comfort of our own preferences. The reference desk was a forced disruption of that curation. It was a place where you could be surprised by a librarian who loved obscure poetry or a librarian who had a strong opinion about local zoning laws.

The kiosk does not surprise. The kiosk confirms. It asks for your barcode. It scans the item. It prints your receipt. It is efficient because it assumes you already know exactly what you want. It treats the book as a commodity, a unit of inventory to be moved from one hand to another. But books are not commodities; they are arguments, stories, and mirrors. When you pick up a book at a kiosk, you are engaging in a solitary act. When you pick up a book recommended by a person, you are engaging in a dialogue that extends beyond the pages.

There is a specific kind of loneliness in the modern library. It is the silence of the stacks, yes, but also the silence of the interface. If you get stuck on a kiosk, if the scanner fails to read the chip, if you are unsure whether a graphic novel qualifies for the adult section, there is no one to turn to. You are left to troubleshoot your own confusion. The friction of the old system—the wait, the walk across the room, the awkward pause while the librarian checked their catalog—was not just waste. It was space. It was room for a conversation to start. "Did you find what you were looking for?" "No, actually, I’m trying to find something that doesn’t make me want to throw my phone into the sea." "Try this one."

We are building a town that values throughput over connection. We want the books delivered to our doorsteps, scanned by apps, and summarized by AI. We want the friction of human interaction smoothed away until it is invisible. But the value of the library was never in the books; it was in the fact that we went there to be in the presence of other people who cared about ideas. The reference desk was the only place in the building where that care was visible.

Now, we have a very quiet room full of very good books, and a row of glowing screens that tell us we are done. We have saved time, but we have lost the chance to be wrong together, to be surprised by a stranger, and to remember that seeking knowledge is still, at its core, a social act. The next time you stand before a kiosk, hesitate. Walk to the desk. Ask the question. Even if the answer is "I don't know," the act of asking is worth more than the silence of the scan.

prompt: Op-ed for a regional paper: our town's library is replacing its reference desk with self-checkout kiosks. Write an essay about what is lost when you stop being able to ask a stranger a question about a book. 600-750 words, no nostalgia porn.
response:
The new signage at the Central Library looks sleek, minimalist, and efficient. It promises "Instant Access" and "24/7 Availability." It is, in every measurable metric, an improvement. The self-checkout kiosks are faster than the reference desk. They do not judge your reading level, they do not take lunch breaks, and they never sigh when you ask for the third book in a series you’ve already read. But in the name of efficiency, we are quietly dismantling a specific, irreplaceable human infrastructure: the ability to ask a stranger a question about a book.

For decades, the reference desk was not just a point of transaction; it was a site of accidental intimacy. It was the one place in a public building where a conversation could start with a query and end with a recommendation that felt like a gift. When you stopped being able to ask that question, you didn’t just lose a librarian; you lost the friction that makes discovery meaningful.

There is a profound difference between searching a database and asking a person. A search algorithm curates based on what you have already consumed. It reinforces your identity, feeding you more of the same. A librarian, however, operates on a different logic. They are trained to listen for the gap in your request. If you ask for "a mystery with a twist," the computer gives you a list of bestsellers. The librarian looks at you, sees that you are a teacher, or a parent, or someone recently divorced, and hands you a book that addresses the twist in a way that resonates with your current life. That exchange requires risk. It requires a stranger to guess correctly about your inner world. When the kiosk replaces the person, the guesswork disappears, and with it, the surprise.
